Built 2026-10-11 on top of [[bmw-decision-studio]]. User asked for the top 5 competitors per series × market, web data (specs, feedback, sales, prices), a competitor-analysis agent and a presenter agent, shown in the report's price region.

- Package `bmw_feedback/competitors/` (registry, snapshot, records, build, engine, facts) + `agents/competition.py`; CLI `python -m bmw_feedback competitors fetch|grep|sources|check|build|analyse`; API `/api/competitors/status|compare`, `/api/agent/competitors`; UI `CompetitorPanel.tsx` + PDF "Competitors" section and "Appendix: competitor sources".
- Rows live in `competitor-data/extracted/*.jsonl` (tracked); raw pages/text in `competitor-data/raw|text` (git-ignored). Every row quotes its saved page; build refuses quotes not in the page or numbers not in the quote. Contract for research agents: `competitor-data/RESEARCH.md`. `00_models.jsonl` is canonical and overrides other batches' model definitions.
- Selection: premium brands only (mainstream → `compact`/`large`, fallback via publisher-named rivals), ranked within the BMW's own segment table of the same publisher (KBA FZ11 segments in DE via `competitor-data/tools/kba_fz11.py`, GoodCarBadCar in US, VFACTS in AU, 16888/CPCA tables in CN), ≥2% of the BMW's volume. RoW = Australia; EU = Germany. F70 not sold in US/CN → no set.
- Prices compared only within one market, currency and price basis (US: MSRP excl. vs incl. destination are different bases). BMW DE side always from its own price list.

**Why:** user wants it done "without mistakes"; the design mirrors the existing rule that the LLM never computes and every claim is verified.

**How to apply / gotchas:** `all` skips the competitor rebuild when snapshots are absent (fresh clone) and uses the tracked CSVs. Never move `competitor-data/raw` while research agents run (it got nested once). Wayback copies of Audi DE price lists are truncated at 5 MiB, so Audi equipment is ADAC-only. KBA counts EQE/EQS/i5/i7/A6 e-tron inside the parent series. The verifier's G70 regex excludes "Genesis G70". Mercedes DE equipment comes from the last published lists (April/July 2024) and is flagged as such. Research subagents repeatedly hit the account session limit; they save incrementally and can be resumed with SendMessage.

# BMW customer feedback: data report and roadmap

**Scope:** BMW 1 Series (F70), 5 Series (G60) and 7 Series (G70) hackathon data.
**Goal:** a pipeline that takes customer feedback about a feature and tells a product manager whether the feature is good or bad, and why.

All numbers in this report are produced by `python -m bmw_feedback all`. They can be checked in `reports/*.csv`, `reports/*.json` and `reports/figures/`.

---

## 1. Summary

1. **The data supports the PM pipeline.**
   - There are 10,128 customer comments, and 8,948 of them carry human labels for three things:
     - which feature the comment is about (VFC level 2, 224 features);
     - whether it is praise, a defect, a usability problem or a request (Feedback Type);
     - why (VFC level 3, 84 reasons).
   - Taken together, these labels are the "good/bad + why" signal.
2. **Never use the raw "% positive".**
   - The four feedback channels have completely different base rates. Source C (a problem survey) contains no praise at all.
   - The models are heard through different channels: the F70 is covered only by Source A.
   - The pipeline therefore scores every feature against what its channel mix predicts. This gives a **complaint index**, where 1.0 means "as expected" (Section 5).
3. **Annotators park praise on umbrella labels.**
   - "Exterior design" has 391 comments and 0 complaints. Specific components almost only collect complaints.
   - Specific features are therefore compared only with other specific features.
4. **Result for the 208 specific features:**

   | Verdict | Features |
   |---|---|
   | Bad | 9 |
   | Leaning bad | 49 |
   | Mixed | 82 |
   | Leaning good | 17 |
   | Good | 9 |
   | Not enough data | 42 |

   - **Clearly bad:** climate control, Personal eSIM, driver profiles, small-item storage.
   - **Clearly good:** seats, My Modes, damping, ambient light, cabin and engine acoustics.
5. **Complaints by domain:**
   - Complaints concentrate in ownership topics (manual, 12 V battery), connected apps, doors/access, infotainment & HMI and EV charging.
   - Chassis & driving dynamics is the clear strength.
   - Drivetrain and exterior also look strong, but mostly through umbrella praise ("great engine", "beautiful design"). Their specific components score about average (Section 4.2).
   - Most complaints are **usability**, not defects: "hard to use / confusing" is the largest reason in every domain except Drivetrain and Interior & storage.
6. **A simple text classifier already routes new comments well.**
   - TF-IDF + logistic regression scores micro-F1 0.81 on feedback type, 0.73 on domain, and 68% top-1 / 87% top-3 on the feature.
   - It degrades when moved to an unseen channel, to 0.64–0.68 on feedback type. That gap is the main thing to fix next (Section 6.2).
7. **Biggest caveats:**
   - The feedback is 92–97% US for G60/G70, and there is no Chinese feedback at all.
   - There are no dates, so trends over time are impossible.
   - Survey and free-text complaints agree only weakly (Spearman rho 0.20).

---

## 2. What is in `BMW-Data/`

| File | Content | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `F70/G60/G70_feedback_hackathon.xlsx` | 13,771 rows. Each row is one (comment, label) pair: ID, Source A–D, Country, model, engine (ICE/BEV/PHEV), Feedback Type, comment text, VFC level-2 + level-3 label | Core training data and verdicts |
| `F70_G60_G68_G70_customer_studies.xlsx` | `CN_EU_2025`: mean satisfaction (0–10) on 37 attributes for EU F70/G60/G70 and CN G68/G70. `US_2025`: 7-point distribution ("I Hate It" … "I Love It") on 103 attributes for G60/G70 | Cross-checking verdicts against structured surveys |
| `sales_volumes.xlsx` | Volume by market (EU, CN, US, RoW) for 2024, 2025 and 2030 per model group | Representativeness and impact weighting |
| `*_OptionList.PDF` | German price lists (July 2026): standard equipment, options with SA code and price, per engine variant | Linking a verdict to price and standard-vs-optional status |

**Repository layout after the clean-up.** The procurement (Demandra) code was moved to the git-ignored `archive/legacy_procurement/` and is also in git history.

```
bmw_feedback/          pipeline package (python -m bmw_feedback ...)
  config.py            paths, constants, verdict thresholds
  taxonomy.py          11 domains <- 224 features; 21 reason families; survey + option-list maps
  load.py              Excel readers (feedback, CN/EU + US survey, sales)
  clean.py             text cleaning, leakage removal, label + comment tables
  scoring.py           channel-adjusted feature verdicts
  classifier.py        TF-IDF + logistic regression (feedback type / domain / feature)
  option_catalog.py    coordinate-aware price-list parser (PyMuPDF), validated on every build
  risk_model.py        explainable boosting machine for complaint drivers
  decision.py          idea -> per series x market recommendation, policy, decision log
  api.py               FastAPI backend for the web app in frontend/
  verdict.py           PM verdict cards (feature name or free text)
  figures.py           all charts in reports/figures/
  cli.py               build | train | figures | export | verdict | serve | all
reports/               REPORT.md, figures, scorecards, metrics (tracked)
data/processed/        cleaned tables (generated, git-ignored)
models/                trained classifiers (generated, git-ignored)
```

The old pipeline's ideas carry over directly:

| Old Demandra idea | BMW equivalent |
|---|---|
| E-Class → +Manufacturer → +Feature cluster | Domain → Feature → Feature + Reason |
| Cold start: borrow from similar buyers | Small features borrow from their domain |
| Economic filter | Volume and market weighting |

---

## 3. Data quality: what was wrong and what the pipeline already fixes

![Comments per model and source](figures/01_data_composition.png)

| # | Issue found | Scale | Fix in `clean.py` / `scoring.py` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Row ≠ comment.** A comment with k labels is repeated k times (up to 17 labels) | 13,771 rows → 10,128 comments; 11.9% of labelled comments are multi-label | Two tidy tables: `labels` (one row per label) and `comments` (one row per comment, label sets as lists). Volumes are counted in comments, not rows |
| 2 | **`no_class_found` placeholder rows.** Most sit next to real labels; 780 comments have nothing else | 2,082 rows | Dropped from labels. The 780 "ncf-only" comments go to the unlabelled pool |
| 3 | **No label at all** (Source D entirely, part of Source C) | 400 comments | Unlabelled pool (1,180 comments in total); classified by the trained model |
| 4 | **Label leakage in Source C.** Text starts with `I had a serious problem with Parking brake - DTU/controls poorly located: "…"` | 571 comments | Prefix stripped; severity (very minor … very serious) and problem code kept as structured columns |
| 5 | **Survey prompts in Source C** ("What is the primary reason for your NPS rating?") | 126 comments | Stripped; prompt type kept |
| 6 | **Template in Source D** ("… That is the one thing I love most / could be most improved about the interior of my vehicle") | 273 comments | Stripped. Topic and stance (213 "love", 60 "improve") kept as weak labels |
| 7 | **Call-centre notes in Source B.** Boilerplate "Customer stated that…", the advisor's reply ("Writer explained…", including typos like "Wrtier") and chatter ("Customer acknowledged.") | 5,479 comments | Removed sentence by sentence |
| 8 | **Casing reveals the channel.** Source A is 99% lowercase, the others 0% | all | Model text is lowercased |
| 9 | **Non-breaking spaces in labels** (`ground\xa0clearance`) | 19 rows | Normalised |
| 10 | **Feedback Type missing although a real label exists** | 18 rows | Imputed from the reason wording ("Not user-friendly" → Difficult to Use) |
| 11 | **"Wants" rows with complaint-worded reasons** ("Dislike: price-performance ratio") | 111 rows | Feedback Type kept as polarity (human judgement of intent); flagged `flag_request_with_complaint_reason` |
| 12 | **EV-only features labelled on ICE cars** (range, charging) | 36 rows | Flagged, not dropped. Usually comparisons with a previous EV or mild-hybrid talk |
| 13 | **Redundant / constant columns** (Brand, Sales Description, `Vfc level2 3 Name`) | n/a | Dropped. `Vfc level2 3 Name` = L2 + " : " + L3 apart from 5 whitespace variants |
| 14 | **Duplicate short notes across IDs** ("he appreciates the touchscreen design.") | 45 texts | Deduplicated before classifier training |
| 15 | **Channel confound.** Source C has 0% Likes; F70 is Source A only | all | Verdicts are standardised by source (Section 5) |
| 16 | **Umbrella-label asymmetry.** Praise goes to "Exterior design", "Drivetrain" etc.; complaints go to components | 16 umbrella labels | Specific features are compared with specific features only |
| 17 | **One empty answer read as missing** (a Source D answer was literally "None.") | 1 | CSVs are read with `keep_default_na=False` |

![Feedback type mix by source](figures/02_feedback_type_by_source.png)

![Label coverage by source](figures/12_label_coverage.png)

### Further cleaning, in order of value

1. **Audit level-3 reasons with a small gold set.**
   - Several reasons are clearly misused. On the F70 touch screen, "Damage" is used for *software crashes*, and "Size not user friendly" (62 rows) is really "touch-only operation / missing rotary dial".
   - One "Electric Range" request is actually about heating controls.
   - Re-label ~300 stratified comments, measure agreement, and fix systematic mappings in `taxonomy.REASON_FAMILIES`.
2. **Split multi-aspect comments into clauses before labelling or scoring.**
   - 1,066 comments carry several labels, but the polarity is per comment, not per aspect. "Great ride, but the screen is distracting" gives both features both sentiments.
   - Sentence/clause segmentation plus aspect assignment (Section 6.3) removes this noise from the verdicts.
3. **Use Source D's stance as a weak label.** The trained classifier calls 51 of the 213 "love" answers complaints. For example, "Doors pop open automatically as I walk up with the keyfob" is predicted as a Defect. The stance would correct these for free.
4. **Normalise third-person pronouns and the remaining narrative glue in Source B** ("he would like…") if a model is trained on mixed channels. Source A is first-person. Pronoun style is another channel fingerprint.
5. **Check translation artefacts in JP/KR comments.** These include `・` bullets, ▶, and odd phrasing ("the driving feel is firm and moist"). Keep a `language_origin` flag so translated text can be down-weighted or modelled separately.
6. **De-duplicate near-identical comments across IDs.** Use MinHash or cosine similarity > 0.9 to catch copy-paste notes beyond exact duplicates.
7. **Spell-correct conservatively** ("satsifying", "experiance", "dor handles"). Character n-grams already absorb most of this, so it matters mainly for keyword search and LLM prompts.
8. **Get dates.** Without a timestamp you cannot see whether an OTA update fixed CarPlay, or split pre- and post-facelift. This is the single most valuable field to request from BMW.
9. **Get the option code per vehicle (VIN-level build data).** Today you cannot tell whether a customer complaining about the HUD actually has the HUD. That matters for "is the option worth its price".

---

## 4. The categories

### 4.1 Three-level taxonomy (`bmw_feedback/taxonomy.py`)

| Level | What | Count | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Domain | Product area a PM owns | 11 | Hand-curated grouping of VFC level-2 |
| Feature | VFC level-2 label | 224 (16 umbrella + 208 specific) | Data |
| Reason | VFC level-3 label → reason family | 84 → 21 families | Data + hand-curated grouping |

The 11 domains are:

- Drivetrain & Performance
- Chassis & Driving Dynamics
- EV Charging & Range
- Driver Assistance & Safety
- Infotainment & HMI
- Connected Apps & Digital Services
- Seats, Comfort & Climate
- Interior Design & Storage
- Exterior Design & Body
- Doors, Access & Keys
- Ownership & Service

Reason families are split by polarity:

- **Positive:** function works well, performance & efficiency, easy to use, design & craftsmanship, comfort & space, sound, good value.
- **Negative:** hard to use, cannot be switched off, inaccurate information, malfunction / software fault, battery drain, build quality / damage, noise & vibration, performance / range shortfall, uncomfortable / too small, poor value / missing equipment.
- **Requests:** new function, easier use, different design/material, more performance/comfort.

### 4.2 Domain view

![Domain overview](figures/03_domain_overview.png)

| Domain | Comments | Complaint index | Verdict | Defect vs usability mentions |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Ownership & Service | 183 | 1.78 | Bad | 30 / 92 |
| Connected Apps & Digital Services | 295 | 1.58 | Bad | 48 / 161 |
| Doors, Access & Keys | 636 | 1.55 | Bad | 193 / 253 |
| Infotainment & HMI | 1,482 | 1.51 | Bad | 303 / 676 |
| EV Charging & Range | 432 | 1.41 | Bad | 53 / 194 |
| Driver Assistance & Safety | 867 | 1.22 | Leaning bad | 119 / 308 |
| Seats, Comfort & Climate | 967 | 1.04 | Mixed | 130 / 305 |
| Interior Design & Storage | 891 | 0.88 | Mixed | 92 / 239 |
| Exterior Design & Body | 1,280 | 0.79 | Good | 169 / 208 |
| Drivetrain & Performance | 1,602 | 0.64 | Good | 132 / 259 |
| Chassis & Driving Dynamics | 1,913 | 0.45 | Good | 126 / 213 |

**Robustness check: the same domain scores on specific features only.** Umbrella praise sits mostly in Chassis, Drivetrain and Exterior, so the table above flatters those domains. Re-scoring with umbrella labels removed gives a ranking that correlates at Spearman 0.79 with the one above:

- The three most-complained-about domains stay on top: Connected Apps 1.22, Ownership & Service 1.21, Doors, Access & Keys 1.15.
- Chassis & Driving Dynamics stays the best domain (0.82, Leaning good).
- **Exterior Design & Body falls from Good (0.79) to Mixed (1.08).** Customers praise the *design* in general, but specific exterior parts (mirrors, lighting, wipers) collect average or above-average complaints.
- **Drivetrain** moves to Mixed (0.96).
- **Seats, Comfort & Climate** improves to Leaning good (0.83).

Use the umbrella-inclusive view for "what do customers love about the car" and the specific-only view for "which components need work".

![Complaint reasons by domain](figures/06_complaint_reasons_by_domain.png)

![Domain by model](figures/07_domain_by_model.png)

**Model differences worth a PM's attention:**

- **F70 infotainment** has a complaint index of 2.02, against 1.29 for G60 and 1.38 for G70. The feature-level breakdown shows why: the F70 touch screen is rated **Bad (1.26)** while the G60's is **Good (0.70)**. F70 owners miss the rotary controller and physical buttons.
- **F70 doors & access** is at 1.98 and **F70 seats & climate** at 1.28, both worse than the larger cars.
- **G70 climate control** is "Bad" (1.43, n=43) against 1.16 on the G60. The US survey agrees: 18% of G70 owners rate climate performance "Unsatisfactory" or worse, against 5.6% for the G60.
- **G70 Personal eSIM** is "Bad" (1.76, n=39). Across all models, 33 of 46 eSIM complaint labels are "Not user-friendly", and the quotes point to being tied to a single US carrier.

### 4.3 Feature view

![Feature health map](figures/04_feature_health_map.png)

![Top 30 features](figures/05_top_features.png)

The full table is `reports/feature_scorecard.csv`: one row per feature with observed/expected counts, indices, 95% intervals, channel-adjusted shares, Defect vs Difficult-to-Use counts and the verdict.

"""Agent 2 - Explainer: fact bundle -> a decision brief for a BMW product manager.

The model (OPENAI_EXPLAINER_MODEL) sees only the facts (ID | deterministic
sentence) and the PM's confirmed scope. Every claim it writes must cite fact
IDs; the verifier then checks each claim against those facts.
"""

from .contracts import SECTIONS, Claim, ExplanationLLM, FactBundle, IdeaSpec, MOVE_LABELS
from .facts import fact_lines
from .llm import LLMOutputInvalid

INSTRUCTIONS = """You are the explanation agent of BMW's product-idea evaluator. Your reader is a BMW product manager deciding whether and where to pursue an idea for the 1 Series (F70), 5 Series (G60) and 7 Series (G70).

You receive FACTS, one per line as "ID | statement". They come from processed customer feedback, the 2025 customer studies, sales volumes, the German price lists and the outputs of trained models. They are your only source of truth.

Write a decision brief:
- headline: one sentence with the bottom line - where the idea is worth pursuing, where not, or that the evidence is insufficient.
- customer_evidence: 2-4 claims on what customers say (verdicts, complaint / request indices, top reasons; a short verbatim quote if it helps).
- market_view: 2-4 claims on where it matters by series and market (recommendations, scores, sales volumes, survey ranks).
- price_and_equipment: 1-3 claims on today's fitment and price and what the proposed move implies.
- risks_and_caveats: 1-3 claims on the limits of the evidence (thin or borrowed data, missing markets, caveats).
- next_steps: 1-3 concrete actions the facts motivate.

Rules - a verifier checks every claim and deletes those that break them:
1. Each claim lists in fact_ids every fact whose number, label, quote, series or market it uses.
2. Use only numbers written in the cited facts, at the same or fewer decimals. Never add, subtract, average, convert or count yourself; if you need a count, difference or share, cite the fact that states it.
3. Write recommendation and verdict labels in single quotes exactly as the facts do, e.g. 'Prioritise', 'Leaning bad'.
4. Put a customer's words in double quotes only when copied exactly from a cited comment fact.
5. Name a series or market only when a cited fact is about it. Write '1 Series (F70)', '5 Series (G60)', '7 Series (G70)', 'Europe', 'United States', 'China', 'Rest of world'.
6. No causes, forecasts, competitors or general knowledge the facts do not state. If evidence is thin or missing, say so plainly.
7. Short, direct sentences for a busy manager. No filler, no marketing language. One idea per claim."""


def _scope(spec: IdeaSpec) -> str:
    feats = ", ".join(f.feature for f in spec.features) or "none (no matching feature in the data)"
    return (f"IDEA: {spec.idea}\nPM-CONFIRMED SCOPE: features {feats}; series {', '.join(spec.series) or 'all'}; "
            f"markets {', '.join(spec.markets) or 'all'}; move {MOVE_LABELS[spec.move]}; proposed price "
            f"{'EUR ' + format(spec.proposed_price_eur, ',.0f') if spec.proposed_price_eur else 'none'}.")


def write(llm, bundle: FactBundle, spec: IdeaSpec, feedback: list[Claim] | None = None) -> ExplanationLLM:
    text = f"{_scope(spec)}\n\nFACTS (ID | statement):\n{fact_lines(bundle)}"
    if feedback:
        lines = []
        for c in feedback:
            failed = "; ".join(f"{ch.name}: {ch.detail}" for ch in c.checks if not ch.passed)
            lines.append(f"- [{c.section}] \"{c.text}\" (cited {', '.join(c.fact_ids) or 'nothing'}) -> {failed}")
        text += ("\n\nYOUR PREVIOUS DRAFT FAILED VERIFICATION FOR THESE CLAIMS. Rewrite the whole brief. Fix each claim "
                 "so that it follows the rules, or drop it:\n" + "\n".join(lines))
    draft = llm.parse("explainer", INSTRUCTIONS, text, ExplanationLLM)
    if not draft.headline.text.strip():
        raise LLMOutputInvalid("The explainer returned an empty headline.", ["headline.text: empty"])
    return draft


def to_claims(draft: ExplanationLLM, attempt: int) -> list[Claim]:
    claims, n = [], 0
    for section in SECTIONS:
        items = [draft.headline] if section == "headline" else getattr(draft, section)
        for c in items:
            if not c.text.strip():          # an empty claim says nothing; drop it rather than verify it
                continue
            n += 1
            ids = list(dict.fromkeys(i.strip() for i in c.fact_ids if i.strip()))
            claims.append(Claim(id=f"c{n}", section=section, text=c.text.strip(), fact_ids=ids, attempt=attempt))
    return claims

Written for: you and a teammate pitching live to the BMW jury. The script is what you say on stage; the rest is prep notes for the two of you.

# 3-minute pitch: Decision Studio

I ran both demo ideas through your local app (agents, scoring, brief and fact-check) on `127.0.0.1:8000`. Every number in the script appears on screen.

## Which ideas to demo

| | Idea to type | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Main** | **"Fix the climate control on the 7 Series"** | It covers all five criteria in one run. The verdict is Bad, US is Prioritise from two independent sources, Europe is labelled "borrowed", and China is a conflict the app refuses to resolve. The brief came back in 15 s with 18 of 18 sentences verified. |
| **Closer** | **"A built-in vacuum for pet hair"** (already an example chip) | The retriever picks no feature, and the brief opens with "Evidence is insufficient to decide…". This is your "We reward honesty" moment. |

## Before you go on stage
1. **Run the demo locally, not on Render.** `munich-ehl-finale.onrender.com` did not answer within 60 s when I tried it.
2. **Pre-run both ideas in two browser tabs.** The brief takes 15–32 s, which is too long to wait for live. Keep the exported PDF as a fallback.
3. **The LLM's wording can vary between runs.** Read the verified-sentence count off your pre-run tab and say that number.
4. **`data/decisions.jsonl` holds 4 test entries.** One is a "helicopter rotors" idea marked *accept* with the rationale "I dont want to do it". Clear it before the demo if you'll show the log. I left it alone because it isn't mine to delete.

---

## The script (~390 spoken words, about 2:50)
**SPEAKER** talks. **DRIVER** clicks. One person can do both.

**0:00 · Hook** *(DRIVER: landing page, nothing typed yet)*
> *(slowly, then pause)* "'Even with Max A/C selected, the interior takes a long time to cool down.'
> That's a real 7 Series owner. One of ten thousand voices in BMW's data.
> So: is that one unhappy customer, or a requirement for the next 7 Series?
> Today that answer hides in four separate data sources. We answer it in under a minute. And at the end, we'll show you the moment our AI says: *'I don't know.'*"

**0:20 · What it is**
> "Decision Studio links BMW's customer feedback, customer studies, sales volumes and price lists, plus competitor data from the web, into one knowledge graph. Every node points back to its source."

**0:30 · AI step, then human gate 1** *(DRIVER: Process view, steps 1–2)*
> "A PM types an idea. Agent one maps it to BMW's feedback taxonomy, and it flags its own gap: the exact issue isn't stated. Then human gate one: nothing runs until the PM confirms the scope."

**0:45 · Scoring (Decision & Scoring Logic)** *(DRIVER: Metrics tab, click G70 US)*
> "Now the scoring, and here no AI is allowed. It's deterministic Python with four signals: complaints, how widely the issue is raised, explicit requests and survey weakness, all weighted by sales volume.
> We never use raw complaint counts, because one of BMW's feedback channels contains zero praise. So each complaint count is compared to what its channel predicts.
> 7 Series in the US: forty-two percent more complaints than expected, and the confidence interval rules out chance. The US customer study agrees on its own: climate ranks 71st of 103 attributes. Two sources, one verdict: **Prioritise**.
> *(DRIVER: open 'Adjust the decision policy', move a weight)* Disagree with our weights? Change them. The scores recompute instantly, and the policy gets a new hash. Same data plus same policy gives the same answer for every PM."

**1:20 · Write and fact-check (Traceability)** *(DRIVER: Summary, open the brief, click a citation)*
> "Only now does an LLM write. Every sentence has to cite its facts. A verifier checks each one: the numbers, the quotes, the scope. Then a second model confirms that the facts really support the sentence. A sentence that fails gets one rewrite, and then it's deleted. Here, [18 of 18] are verified. Click any citation and you go straight to the source."

**1:45 · Uncertainty and conflict (the honesty criterion)** *(DRIVER: Metrics, click G70 EU, then G70 CN)*
> "Now watch how it handles uncertainty. Europe has *one* comment, so the verdict is borrowed at half weight and labelled 'borrowed'. China's survey calls climate a *strength*, but there are zero Chinese comments. We don't average that conflict into a fake number. It says: *insufficient evidence, collect China feedback first.*"

**2:10 · Human gate 2 (Workflow & Audit)** *(DRIVER: step 6, decision form)*
> "Human gate two: the PM follows or overrides, and never without a written rationale. The decision is logged with the policy hash and a fingerprint of the exact data files, so you can reconstruct it months later."

**2:25 · The promised moment** *(DRIVER: switch to the vacuum tab)*
> "And here's the moment I promised. A built-in vacuum for pet hair. There's zero evidence in the data, and the app says exactly that instead of inventing demand."

**2:40 · Close (Scale & Impact)**
> "The briefing asked for one vehicle in one market. We cover three series in four markets. AI proposes. The data sets the score. The PM decides. *(pause)* From billions of findings to one BMW."

If you run long, cut the "Disagree with our weights?" line. Don't cut the China line: it's your strongest moment for the honesty criterion.

---

## How the script covers the criteria
| Criterion | Where | What's on screen |
|---|---|---|
| Decision & Scoring Logic | 0:45 | Four weighted signals, channel-adjusted index with confidence interval, policy hash |
| Workflow & Human Decision | 0:30 / 2:10 | AI → gate 1 → no-AI engine → AI plus verifier → gate 2 |
| Traceability & Auditability | 1:20 / 2:10 | Citation → fact → graph node; decision log with policy and data hashes |
| Quality, Usability, Feasibility | throughout | Plain-language brief that a PM can act on in under a minute |
| Innovation & Scale | 0:20 / 2:40 | Knowledge graph, web competitor data, 3 series × 4 markets |
| "We reward honesty" | 1:45 / 2:25 | Borrowed label, China conflict, the vacuum idea |

## Q&A cheat sheet
- **"Why not just let GPT rank?"** "The LLM never calculates. Python does all the scoring, so the same inputs always give the same output, with hashes to prove it."
- **"Conflicting signals?"** "We score each series and market separately and never average across them. Survey scores and free-text complaints only agree weakly in this data, so we show both side by side."
- **"Is the feedback representative?"** "No. 5 and 7 Series feedback is mostly US, and there's none from China. That's why every cell shows its evidence coverage, and why the China cells refuse to recommend."
- **"Where's the requirement list?"** "All 208 specific features are already ranked by verdict. Climate control, Personal eSIM, driver profiles and small-item storage are the worst. Each evaluation is a drill-down into one of them."
- **"LLM down?"** "Scoring, evidence and the graph still work. The brief shows as unavailable, and nothing is pre-recorded."
- **"Business impact numbers?"** Don't make one up. Say: "Four sources answered in under a minute, with an auditable record. We'd measure time-to-decision in a pilot."

## Gaps: don't claim these in the pitch
1. **Postpone and reject don't exist.** The decision form only offers follow or override, and the traceability criterion names "postponements and rejections" explicitly. Adding them is a small change to the decision form and the decision log, and I can do it now if you want.
2. **There's no requirements backlog with IDs.** The app evaluates ideas the PM brings rather than generating a list. Use the ranked-features answer above. A backup slide using the briefing's requirement fields (ID, description, sources, priority, rationale, evidence level, assumptions, status) would also help.
3. **The app doesn't define measurable targets or acceptance criteria.** BMW's process slide includes them, so don't say it does.
4. **Only the US is Prioritise on direct evidence.** Never say "Prioritise in Europe" without adding "borrowed". A judge who clicks Europe will see it rests on one comment.

Format is a separate matter: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. A Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title, uses almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages don't need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

Distinctive choices come from the subject's own world: its materials, instruments, and vernacular. Whatever the treatment, include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament; it costs nothing even on a plain page. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (about 400px). Give images and any `aspect-ratio` box `max-width: 100%`, and don't give anything a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only wide tables, code, and diagrams may exceed it; give each `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere except a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content stays clear of the system bars; keep that padding. A bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding. A sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` and never `0`. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` instead of `100vh`, so it fits inside that padding. A page that includes its own viewport meta gets this padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Make repeated elements consistent.** For cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, or badges on sibling items, use the same edges, baselines, and inner padding on each, and put any recurring element in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over empty space or sits alone in a row. Make text that can outgrow its track wrap or scroll in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Use card styling selectively.** Border, fill, radius, and shadow each mark an element as a separate object. Apply them by role, to set off the one element that needs it; applying the same radius and shadow to every block flattens the hierarchy. Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

Color chart text from the theme tokens so it is readable in both themes. Keep marks, labels, and edges clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds; in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Make the page complete at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, with no scrolling to trigger it; that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all see. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never left at `opacity: 0` waiting for an observer. Size a hero to its content instead of to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the rest of the page out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state: the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, or a plausibly filled form, clearly marked as examples and never presented as the user's own figures. The first view shows what the tool does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing. When those records live in the `db` capability, keep them out of the page source. Its first frame renders before the store answers, so make that frame a designed empty state that names what will appear and how to add the first entry, then fill it from the store. Seed the store through the `ArtifactData` tool (what type instructions call `write_db`) after the first publish: the user's real data, or marked examples for a tool only the user will use. For a store other people will fill with their own entries, seed only what the user gave you or asked for, never invented people or records.

**Avoid AI-generated design.** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. When the user specifies a visual direction, follow it exactly; their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. When nothing is specified, don't use that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly.** Watch for overlapping elements, cascade collisions, and silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform preserves form values, focus, and scroll position across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, use Canvas or WebGL instead of hand-writing long SVG path data.

**CSS rules.** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificity. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out, e.g. a type-based selector like `.section` and an element-based one like `.cta` both setting padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't undo your spacing unnoticed.

**Writing the copy.** Treat words as design material and never as decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen: name things by what people recognize instead of how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*; they don't manage *webhook config*). Use active voice; a control states exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it, without apologies or vagueness. Prefer specific to clever. Write plainly, the way a knowledgeable person would talk. Avoid mannered devices: asides set off by em-dashes, "not X, but Y" framing, colon-then-reveal sentences, scare quotes around invented labels, and stock phrases such as "worth noting" or "honest caveat". Prefer short, direct sentences over compressed or clever phrasing.

**Name the page like a product; don't caption it.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it gives the reader a first impression of the care taken. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject; or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which then is the page's name. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Stop at the name; a title that adds its own explanation after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it appears beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could apply to any of them fails as a name just as an appended explanation does. When a candidate title combines the name with a generic word (a greeting, a category, a page-type label), keep the name; a trim that drops the identifying part and keeps the generic word produces a title that could apply to any page. This rule removes explanations and doesn't require brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. Put the explanation in the one-sentence publish `description`; the gallery shows it directly under the title.

**Structure is information.** Structural devices (numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels) should encode something true about the content instead of decorating it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but those fit only if the content actually is a sequence, such as a real process or a typed timeline where the order is information the reader needs. Before adding numbered markers or similar devices, check that they actually make sense.

**When the page is a UI (dashboard, tool).** It is scanned and operated instead of read top to bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Put the summary before the detail. Encode state in form as well as in numbers (a pill, a chip, a severity stripe) so that whatever needs attention is visible at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. Interactive elements should look interactive.



## Process

Start from what the viewer should be able to do on the page, in addition to what they will read. If the page should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user. A page that is only read doesn't need that.

Before writing the page, settle a short design plan (a compact token system) and write it into the file itself, as the `:root` block at the top of the page's `<style>`, rather than into your reply:
- **Color**: the palette as 4-6 named color tokens.
- **Type**: font tokens for 2+ roles: a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: the layout concept as a one-line comment above the tokens.

Then build the rest of the page from those tokens, deriving every color and type decision from them. The plan is working material, not part of the answer: unless the user asks about the design, one plain sentence on the direction is the most to say about it, with no hex values or font names.

**Write, check once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way: one `ArtifactCheck` preview (or the Artifact tool's own `action: "preview"` where there is no separate `ArtifactCheck` tool), or else one screenshot of the local file; if the session offers none of these, skip the look. The preview renders desktop and phone widths in light and dark and lists overflow, colors that ignore the theme, blocked loads and console errors, including a script that fails to parse, so nothing it covers needs a check of your own. The look is optional: if you take it, make one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look; then publish. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring, parsing) may get one more check before publishing: one run of a pure function on a sample input, or, where no preview ran, one syntax check of its script; nothing more. A page that declares `capabilities` takes the look rather than skipping it, then one functional pass after the first publish, because the preview cannot run that code: read back once what the page stores or serves (one read of its stored data or one read-only route call; where that read alone would prove nothing, as on an empty store, you may first write one probe document yourself and delete it after the read, passing the `version` the write returned as `if_version`; no other test writes unless the user wants one), tell the user in one line what you exercised and what you could not, and stop. None of this becomes a loop, because the user is waiting for a link: no second screenshot, no scripts that probe the DOM, no re-running a check that passed. Review happens on the live page, and further polish is for the user to request; if the user reports something visibly broken (a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing), fix that, take at most one more look if the session offers a way, and republish once. These checks are for code you wrote into this page, not for content you fill into an Artifact made from an Artifact type (a Slides deck, a Design canvas): there the type's own instructions say whether to check, and if they say nothing, don't.

**Open viewers.** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open: published changes are delivered to them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state preserved where possible. If your page has state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`; `hot` is the viewer's own update hook, not a capability behind `claude.use()`, and is absent outside a viewer, hence the `?.`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance changes here: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated decisions, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part in the plan itself, without narrating the revision to the user. Write the code only after the plan is specific to this subject, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero states the thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world (headline, image, live demo, interactive moment). 
- Typography sets the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, avoiding the families you would use on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design instead of a neutral container for the content. 
- Use motion deliberately. Think about whether and where animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. One orchestrated moment is usually more effective than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation adds to the impression that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Put your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent clashes with the background, shift it toward an analogous hue or desaturate it instead of replacing it.

Munich EHL Finale · BMW challenge · 3-minute slot

Decision Studio pitch

The spoken script, the demo choices and the prep notes for presenting to the BMW jury. Every number in the script was checked against a local run of the app.

~390 spoken words about 2:50 2 roles: Speaker, Driver

Which ideas to demo

Main demo · type it

Fix the climate control on the 7 Series

It covers all five criteria in one run. The verdict is Bad, US is Prioritise from two independent sources, Europe is labelled “borrowed”, and China is a conflict the app refuses to resolve. The brief came back in 15 s with 18 of 18 sentences verified.

Closer · example chip

A built-in vacuum for pet hair

The retriever picks no feature, and the brief opens with “Evidence is insufficient to decide…”. This is your “We reward honesty” moment.

Before you go on stage

  1. Run the demo locally, not on Render. munich-ehl-finale.onrender.com did not answer within 60 s when it was tested.
  2. Pre-run both ideas in two browser tabs. The brief takes 15–32 s, which is too long to wait for live. Keep the exported PDF as a fallback.
  3. The LLM’s wording can vary between runs. Read the verified-sentence count off your pre-run tab and say that number.
  4. data/decisions.jsonl holds 4 test entries. One is a “helicopter rotors” idea marked accept with the rationale “I dont want to do it”. Clear it before the demo if you’ll show the log.

The script

Speaker says the serif lines Driver does the mono cues One person can do both.
  1. 0:00

    Hook

    DriverLanding page, nothing typed yet

    (slowly, then pause) “‘Even with Max A/C selected, the interior takes a long time to cool down.’

    That’s a real 7 Series owner. One of ten thousand voices in BMW’s data.

    So: is that one unhappy customer, or a requirement for the next 7 Series?

    Today that answer hides in four separate data sources. We answer it in under a minute. And at the end, we’ll show you the moment our AI says: ‘I don’t know.’”

  2. 0:20

    What it is

    “Decision Studio links BMW’s customer feedback, customer studies, sales volumes and price lists, plus competitor data from the web, into one knowledge graph. Every node points back to its source.”

  3. 0:30

    AI step, then human gate 1 Workflow

    DriverProcess view, steps 1–2

    “A PM types an idea. Agent one maps it to BMW’s feedback taxonomy, and it flags its own gap: the exact issue isn’t stated. Then human gate one: nothing runs until the PM confirms the scope.”

  4. 0:45

    Scoring Decision & Scoring Logic

    DriverMetrics tab, click G70 US

    “Now the scoring, and here no AI is allowed. It’s deterministic Python with four signals: complaints, how widely the issue is raised, explicit requests and survey weakness, all weighted by sales volume.

    We never use raw complaint counts, because one of BMW’s feedback channels contains zero praise. So each complaint count is compared to what its channel predicts.

    7 Series in the US: forty-two percent more complaints than expected, and the confidence interval rules out chance. The US customer study agrees on its own: climate ranks 71st of 103 attributes. Two sources, one verdict: Prioritise.

    Driver: open ‘Adjust the decision policy’, move a weight Disagree with our weights? Change them. The scores recompute instantly, and the policy gets a new hash. Same data plus same policy gives the same answer for every PM.”

  5. 1:20

    Write and fact-check Traceability

    DriverSummary, open the brief, click a citation

    “Only now does an LLM write. Every sentence has to cite its facts. A verifier checks each one: the numbers, the quotes, the scope. Then a second model confirms that the facts really support the sentence. A sentence that fails gets one rewrite, and then it’s deleted. Here, 18 of 18 are verified. Click any citation and you go straight to the source.”

  6. 1:45

    Uncertainty and conflict Honesty

    DriverMetrics, click G70 EU, then G70 CN

    “Now watch how it handles uncertainty. Europe has one comment, so the verdict is borrowed at half weight and labelled ‘borrowed’. China’s survey calls climate a strength, but there are zero Chinese comments. We don’t average that conflict into a fake number. It says: insufficient evidence, collect China feedback first.”

  7. 2:10

    Human gate 2 Workflow & Audit

    DriverStep 6, decision form

    “Human gate two: the PM follows or overrides, and never without a written rationale. The decision is logged with the policy hash and a fingerprint of the exact data files, so you can reconstruct it months later.”

  8. 2:25

    The promised moment Honesty

    DriverSwitch to the vacuum tab

    “And here’s the moment I promised. A built-in vacuum for pet hair. There’s zero evidence in the data, and the app says exactly that instead of inventing demand.”

  9. 2:40

    Close Scale & Impact

    “The briefing asked for one vehicle in one market. We cover three series in four markets. AI proposes. The data sets the score. The PM decides. (pause) From billions of findings to one BMW.”

If you run long, cut the “Disagree with our weights?” line. Don’t cut the China line: it’s your strongest moment for the honesty criterion.

How the script covers the criteria

CriterionWhereWhat’s on screen
Decision & Scoring Logic0:45Four weighted signals, channel-adjusted index with confidence interval, policy hash
Workflow & Human Decision0:30 / 2:10AI → gate 1 → no-AI engine → AI plus verifier → gate 2
Traceability & Auditability1:20 / 2:10Citation → fact → graph node; decision log with policy and data hashes
Quality, Usability, FeasibilitythroughoutPlain-language brief that a PM can act on in under a minute
Innovation & Scale0:20 / 2:40Knowledge graph, web competitor data, 3 series × 4 markets
“We reward honesty”1:45 / 2:25Borrowed label, China conflict, the vacuum idea

Q&A cheat sheet

“Why not just let GPT rank?”
“The LLM never calculates. Python does all the scoring, so the same inputs always give the same output, with hashes to prove it.”
“Conflicting signals?”
“We score each series and market separately and never average across them. Survey scores and free-text complaints only agree weakly in this data, so we show both side by side.”
“Is the feedback representative?”
“No. 5 and 7 Series feedback is mostly US, and there’s none from China. That’s why every cell shows its evidence coverage, and why the China cells refuse to recommend.”
“Where’s the requirement list?”
“All 208 specific features are already ranked by verdict. Climate control, Personal eSIM, driver profiles and small-item storage are the worst. Each evaluation is a drill-down into one of them.”
“LLM down?”
“Scoring, evidence and the graph still work. The brief shows as unavailable, and nothing is pre-recorded.”
“Business impact numbers?”
Don’t make one up. Say: “Four sources answered in under a minute, with an auditable record. We’d measure time-to-decision in a pilot.”

Gaps: don’t claim these in the pitch

  1. Postpone and reject don’t exist. The decision form only offers follow or override, and the traceability criterion names “postponements and rejections” explicitly. Adding them is a small change to the decision form and the decision log.
  2. There’s no requirements backlog with IDs. The app evaluates ideas the PM brings rather than generating a list. Use the ranked-features answer above. A backup slide using the briefing’s requirement fields (ID, description, sources, priority, rationale, evidence level, assumptions, status) would also help.
  3. The app doesn’t define measurable targets or acceptance criteria. BMW’s process slide includes them, so don’t say it does.
  4. Only the US is Prioritise on direct evidence. Never say “Prioritise in Europe” without adding “borrowed”. A judge who clicks Europe will see it rests on one comment.

This page contains BMW figures and a verbatim customer quote. Keep the link inside the team and don’t paste it into the public repo.

Numbers checked against a local run of the app on 11 October 2026. The written brief comes from an LLM, so its wording and sentence count can differ on your run.
